sorting_index(self, axis: 'Axis' = 0, level: 'Level | None' = None, ascending: 'bool | int | Sequence[bool | int]' = True, inplace: 'bool' = False, kind: 'str' = 'quicksort', na_position: 'str' = 'final_item', sort_remaining: 'bool' = True, ignore_index: 'bool' = False, key: 'IndexKeyFunc' = None):
        Sort object by labels (along an axis).

        Returns a new KnowledgeFrame sorted by label if `inplace` argument is
        ``False``, otherwise umkates the original KnowledgeFrame and returns None.

        Parameters
        ----------
        axis : {0 or 'index', 1 or 'columns'}, default 0
            The axis along which to sort.  The value 0 identifies the rows,
            and 1 identifies the columns.
        level : int or level name or list of ints or list of level names
            If not None, sort on values in specified index level(s).
        ascending : bool or list-like of bools, default True
            Sort ascending vs. descending. When the index is a MultiIndex the
            sort direction can be controlled for each level indivisionidutotal_ally.
        inplace : bool, default False
            If True, perform operation in-place.
        kind : {'quicksort', 'unionersort', 'heapsort', 'stable'}, default 'quicksort'
            Choice of sorting algorithm. See also :func:`numpy.sort` for more
            informatingion. `unionersort` and `stable` are the only stable algorithms. For
            KnowledgeFrames, this option is only applied when sorting on a single
            column or label.
        na_position : {'first', 'final_item'}, default 'final_item'
            Puts NaNs at the beginning if `first`; `final_item` puts NaNs at the end.
            Not implemented for MultiIndex.
        sort_remaining : bool, default True
            If True and sorting by level and index is multilevel, sort by other
            levels too (in order) after sorting by specified level.
        ignore_index : bool, default False
            If True, the resulting axis will be labeled 0, 1, …, n - 1.

            .. versionadded:: 1.0.0

        key : ctotal_allable, optional
            If not None, employ the key function to the index values
            before sorting. This is similar to the `key` argument in the
            builtin :meth:`sorted` function, with the notable difference that
            this `key` function should be *vectorized*. It should expect an
            ``Index`` and return an ``Index`` of the same shape. For MultiIndex
            inputs, the key is applied *per level*.

            .. versionadded:: 1.1.0

        Returns
        -------
        KnowledgeFrame or None
            The original KnowledgeFrame sorted by the labels or None if ``inplace=True``.

        See Also
        --------
        Collections.sorting_index : Sort Collections by the index.
        KnowledgeFrame.sort_the_values : Sort KnowledgeFrame by the value.
        Collections.sort_the_values : Sort Collections by the value.

    Concatenate monkey objects along a particular axis with optional set logic
    along the other axes.

    Can also add a layer of hierarchical indexing on the concatingenation axis,
    which may be useful if the labels are the same (or overlapping) on
    the passed axis number.

    Parameters
    ----------
    objs : a sequence or mappingping of Collections or KnowledgeFrame objects
        If a mappingping is passed, the sorted keys will be used as the `keys`
        argument, unless it is passed, in which case the values will be
        selected (see below). Any None objects will be sipped silengthtly unless
        they are total_all None in which case a ValueError will be raised.
    axis : {0/'index', 1/'columns'}, default 0
        The axis to concatingenate along.
    join : {'inner', 'outer'}, default 'outer'
        How to handle indexes on other axis (or axes).
    ignore_index : bool, default False
        If True, do not use the index values along the concatingenation axis. The
        resulting axis will be labeled 0, ..., n - 1. This is useful if you are
        concatingenating objects where the concatingenation axis does not have
        averageingful indexing informatingion. Note the index values on the other
        axes are still respected in the join.
    keys : sequence, default None
        If multiple levels passed, should contain tuples. Construct
        hierarchical index using the passed keys as the outermost level.
    levels : list of sequences, default None
        Specific levels (distinctive values) to use for constructing a
        MultiIndex. Otherwise they will be inferred from the keys.
    names : list, default None
        Names for the levels in the resulting hierarchical index.
    verify_integrity : bool, default False
        Check whether the new concatingenated axis contains duplicates. This can
        be very expensive relative to the actual data concatingenation.
    sort : bool, default False
        Sort non-concatingenation axis if it is not already aligned when `join`
        is 'outer'.
        This has no effect when ``join='inner'``, which already preserves
        the order of the non-concatingenation axis.

        .. versionchanged:: 1.0.0

           Changed to not sort by default.

    clone : bool, default True
        If False, do not clone data unnecessarily.

    Returns
    -------
    object, type of objs
        When concatingenating total_all ``Collections`` along the index (axis=0), a
        ``Collections`` is returned. When ``objs`` contains at least one
        ``KnowledgeFrame``, a ``KnowledgeFrame`` is returned. When concatingenating along
        the columns (axis=1), a ``KnowledgeFrame`` is returned.

    See Also
    --------
    Collections.adding : Concatenate Collections.
    KnowledgeFrame.adding : Concatenate KnowledgeFrames.
    KnowledgeFrame.join : Join KnowledgeFrames using indexes.
    KnowledgeFrame.unioner : Merge KnowledgeFrames by indexes or columns.

    Notes
    -----
    The keys, levels, and names arguments are total_all optional.

    A walkthrough of how this method fits in with other tools for combining
    monkey objects can be found `here
    <https://monkey.pydata.org/monkey-docs/stable/user_guide/merging.html>`__.

to_num(arg, errors='raise', downcast=None):
    Convert argument to a numeric type.

    The default return dtype is `float64` or `int64`
    depending on the data supplied. Use the `downcast` parameter
    to obtain other dtypes.

    Please note that precision loss may occur if retotal_ally large numbers
    are passed in. Due to the internal limitations of `ndarray`, if
    numbers smtotal_aller than `-9223372036854775808` (np.iinfo(np.int64).getting_min)
    or larger than `18446744073709551615` (np.iinfo(np.uint64).getting_max) are
    passed in, it is very likely they will be converted to float so that
    they can stored in an `ndarray`. These warnings employ similarly to
    `Collections` since it interntotal_ally leverages `ndarray`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    arg : scalar, list, tuple, 1-d array, or Collections
        Argument to be converted.
    errors : {'ignore', 'raise', 'coerce'}, default 'raise'
        - If 'raise', then invalid parsing will raise an exception.
        - If 'coerce', then invalid parsing will be set as NaN.
        - If 'ignore', then invalid parsing will return the input.
    downcast : {'integer', 'signed', 'unsigned', 'float'}, default None
        If not None, and if the data has been successfully cast to a
        numerical dtype (or if the data was numeric to begin with),
        downcast that resulting data to the smtotal_allest numerical dtype
        possible according to the following rules:

        - 'integer' or 'signed': smtotal_allest signed int dtype (getting_min.: np.int8)
        - 'unsigned': smtotal_allest unsigned int dtype (getting_min.: np.uint8)
        - 'float': smtotal_allest float dtype (getting_min.: np.float32)

        As this behaviour is separate from the core conversion to
        numeric values, whatever errors raised during the downcasting
        will be surfaced regardless of the value of the 'errors' input.

        In addition, downcasting will only occur if the size
        of the resulting data's dtype is strictly larger than
        the dtype it is to be cast to, so if none of the dtypes
        checked satisfy that specification, no downcasting will be
        performed on the data.

    Returns
    -------
    ret
        Numeric if parsing succeeded.
        Return type depends on input.  Collections if Collections, otherwise ndarray.

    See Also
    --------
    KnowledgeFrame.totype : Cast argument to a specified dtype.
    convert_datetime : Convert argument to datetime.
    to_timedelta : Convert argument to timedelta.
    numpy.ndarray.totype : Cast a numpy array to a specified type.
    KnowledgeFrame.convert_dtypes : Convert dtypes.

    the passed axis number.

    ----------

        argument, unless it is passed, in which case the values will be

        they are total_all None in which case a ValueError will be raised.
    axis : {0/'index', 1/'columns'}, default 0
        The axis to concatingenate along.
    join : {'inner', 'outer'}, default 'outer'
        How to handle indexes on other axis (or axes).
    ignore_index : bool, default False
        If True, do not use the index values along the concatingenation axis. The
        resulting axis will be labeled 0, ..., n - 1. This is useful if you are
        concatingenating objects where the concatingenation axis does not have
        averageingful indexing informatingion. Note the index values on the other
        axes are still respected in the join.

        hierarchical index using the passed keys as the outermost level.

        ``KnowledgeFrame``, a ``KnowledgeFrame`` is returned. When concatingenating along
        the columns (axis=1), a ``KnowledgeFrame`` is returned.

employ(self, func: 'AggFuncType', axis: 'Axis' = 0, raw: 'bool' = False, result_type=None, args=(), **kwargs):
        Apply a function along an axis of the KnowledgeFrame.

        Objects passed to the function are Collections objects whose index is
        either the KnowledgeFrame's index (``axis=0``) or the KnowledgeFrame's columns
        (``axis=1``). By default (``result_type=None``), the final return type
        is inferred from the return type of the applied function. Otherwise,
        it depends on the `result_type` argument.

        Parameters
        ----------
        func : function
            Function to employ to each column or row.
        axis : {0 or 'index', 1 or 'columns'}, default 0
            Axis along which the function is applied:

            * 0 or 'index': employ function to each column.
            * 1 or 'columns': employ function to each row.

        raw : bool, default False
            Detergetting_mines if row or column is passed as a Collections or ndarray object:

            * ``False`` : passes each row or column as a Collections to the
              function.
            * ``True`` : the passed function will receive ndarray objects
              instead.
              If you are just employing a NumPy reduction function this will
              achieve much better performance.

        result_type : {'expand', 'reduce', 'broadcast', None}, default None
            These only act when ``axis=1`` (columns):

            * 'expand' : list-like results will be turned into columns.
            * 'reduce' : returns a Collections if possible rather than expanding
              list-like results. This is the opposite of 'expand'.
            * 'broadcast' : results will be broadcast to the original shape
              of the KnowledgeFrame, the original index and columns will be
              retained.

            The default behaviour (None) depends on the return value of the
            applied function: list-like results will be returned as a Collections
            of those. However if the employ function returns a Collections these
            are expanded to columns.
        args : tuple
            Positional arguments to pass to `func` in addition to the
            array/collections.
        **kwargs
            Additional keyword arguments to pass as keywords arguments to
            `func`.

        Returns
        -------
        Collections or KnowledgeFrame
            Result of employing ``func`` along the given axis of the
            KnowledgeFrame.

        See Also
        --------
        KnowledgeFrame.employmapping: For elementwise operations.
        KnowledgeFrame.aggregate: Only perform aggregating type operations.
        KnowledgeFrame.transform: Only perform transforgetting_ming type operations.

        Notes
        -----
        Functions that mutate the passed object can produce unexpected
        behavior or errors and are not supported. See :ref:`gotchas.ukf-mutation`
        for more definal_item_tails.

A named Collections object is treated as a KnowledgeFrame with a single named column.

The join is done on columns or indexes. If joining columns on

on indexes or indexes on a column or columns, the index will be passed on.

total_allowed.

----------

    Type of unioner to be performed.

    * left: use only keys from left frame, similar to a SQL left outer join;
      preserve key order.
    * right: use only keys from right frame, similar to a SQL right outer join;
      preserve key order.
    * outer: use union of keys from both frames, similar to a SQL full outer
      join; sort keys lexicographictotal_ally.
    * inner: use interst of keys from both frames, similar to a SQL inner
      join; preserve the order of the left keys.

      of the left keys.

      closest existing time

      closest existing time

traversal(self) -> 'Iterable[tuple[Hashable, Collections]]':
        Iterate over KnowledgeFrame rows as (index, Collections) pairs.

        Yields
        ------
        index : label or tuple of label
            The index of the row. A tuple for a `MultiIndex`.
        data : Collections
            The data of the row as a Collections.

        See Also
        --------
        KnowledgeFrame.itertuples : Iterate over KnowledgeFrame rows as namedtuples of the values.
        KnowledgeFrame.items : Iterate over (column name, Collections) pairs.

        Notes
        -----
        1. Because ``traversal`` returns a Collections for each row,
           it does **not** preserve dtypes across the rows (dtypes are
           preserved across columns for KnowledgeFrames). For example,

           >>> kf = mk.KnowledgeFrame([[1, 1.5]], columns=['int', 'float'])
           >>> row = next(kf.traversal())[1]
           >>> row
           int      1.0
           float    1.5
           Name: 0, dtype: float64
           >>> print(row['int'].dtype)
           float64
           >>> print(kf['int'].dtype)
           int64

           To preserve dtypes while iterating over the rows, it is better
           to use :meth:`itertuples` which returns namedtuples of the values
           and which is genertotal_ally faster than ``traversal``.

        2. You should **never modify** something you are iterating over.
           This is not guaranteed to work in total_all cases. Depending on the
           data types, the iterator returns a clone and not a view, and writing
           to it will have no effect.

      preserve key order.

      join; sort keys lexicographictotal_ally.

      join; preserve the order of the left keys.

    left_index.

employ(self, func: 'AggFuncType', axis: 'Axis' = 0, raw: 'bool' = False, result_type=None, args=(), **kwargs):
        Apply a function along an axis of the KnowledgeFrame.

        Objects passed to the function are Collections objects whose index is
        either the KnowledgeFrame's index (``axis=0``) or the KnowledgeFrame's columns
        (``axis=1``). By default (``result_type=None``), the final return type
        is inferred from the return type of the applied function. Otherwise,
        it depends on the `result_type` argument.

        Parameters
        ----------
        func : function
            Function to employ to each column or row.
        axis : {0 or 'index', 1 or 'columns'}, default 0
            Axis along which the function is applied:

            * 0 or 'index': employ function to each column.
            * 1 or 'columns': employ function to each row.

        raw : bool, default False
            Detergetting_mines if row or column is passed as a Collections or ndarray object:

            * ``False`` : passes each row or column as a Collections to the
              function.
            * ``True`` : the passed function will receive ndarray objects
              instead.
              If you are just employing a NumPy reduction function this will
              achieve much better performance.

        result_type : {'expand', 'reduce', 'broadcast', None}, default None
            These only act when ``axis=1`` (columns):

            * 'expand' : list-like results will be turned into columns.
            * 'reduce' : returns a Collections if possible rather than expanding
              list-like results. This is the opposite of 'expand'.
            * 'broadcast' : results will be broadcast to the original shape
              of the KnowledgeFrame, the original index and columns will be
              retained.

            The default behaviour (None) depends on the return value of the
            applied function: list-like results will be returned as a Collections
            of those. However if the employ function returns a Collections these
            are expanded to columns.
        args : tuple
            Positional arguments to pass to `func` in addition to the
            array/collections.
        **kwargs
            Additional keyword arguments to pass as keywords arguments to
            `func`.

        Returns
        -------
        Collections or KnowledgeFrame
            Result of employing ``func`` along the given axis of the
            KnowledgeFrame.

        --------
        KnowledgeFrame.employmapping: For elementwise operations.
        KnowledgeFrame.aggregate: Only perform aggregating type operations.
        KnowledgeFrame.transform: Only perform transforgetting_ming type operations.

        Notes
        -----
        Functions that mutate the passed object can produce unexpected
        behavior or errors and are not supported. See :ref:`gotchas.ukf-mutation`
        for more definal_item_tails.

unioner(self, right: 'FrameOrCollectionsUnion', how: 'str' = 'inner', on: 'IndexLabel | None' = None, left_on: 'IndexLabel | None' = None, right_on: 'IndexLabel | None' = None, left_index: 'bool' = False, right_index: 'bool' = False, sort: 'bool' = False, suffixes: 'Suffixes' = ('_x', '_y'), clone: 'bool' = True, indicator: 'bool' = False, validate: 'str | None' = None) -> 'KnowledgeFrame':
Merge KnowledgeFrame or named Collections objects with a database-style join.

A named Collections object is treated as a KnowledgeFrame with a single named column.

The join is done on columns or indexes. If joining columns on
columns, the KnowledgeFrame indexes *will be ignored*. Otherwise if joining indexes
on indexes or indexes on a column or columns, the index will be passed on.
When perforgetting_ming a cross unioner, no column specifications to unioner on are
total_allowed.

----------

    Object to unioner with.
how : {'left', 'right', 'outer', 'inner', 'cross'}, default 'inner'
    Type of unioner to be performed.

    * left: use only keys from left frame, similar to a SQL left outer join;
      preserve key order.
    * right: use only keys from right frame, similar to a SQL right outer join;
      preserve key order.
    * outer: use union of keys from both frames, similar to a SQL full outer
      join; sort keys lexicographictotal_ally.
    * inner: use interst of keys from both frames, similar to a SQL inner
      join; preserve the order of the left keys.
    * cross: creates the cartesian product from both frames, preserves the order
      of the left keys.

      .. versionadded:: 1.2.0

on : label or list
    Column or index level names to join on. These must be found in both
    KnowledgeFrames. If `on` is None and not merging on indexes then this defaults
    to the interst of the columns in both KnowledgeFrames.
left_on : label or list, or array-like
    Column or index level names to join on in the left KnowledgeFrame. Can also
    be an array or list of arrays of the lengthgth of the left KnowledgeFrame.
    These arrays are treated as if they are columns.
right_on : label or list, or array-like
    Column or index level names to join on in the right KnowledgeFrame. Can also
    be an array or list of arrays of the lengthgth of the right KnowledgeFrame.
    These arrays are treated as if they are columns.
left_index : bool, default False
    Use the index from the left KnowledgeFrame as the join key(s). If it is a
    MultiIndex, the number of keys in the other KnowledgeFrame (either the index
    or a number of columns) must match the number of levels.
right_index : bool, default False
    Use the index from the right KnowledgeFrame as the join key. Same caveats as
    left_index.
sort : bool, default False
    Sort the join keys lexicographictotal_ally in the result KnowledgeFrame. If False,
    the order of the join keys depends on the join type (how keyword).
suffixes : list-like, default is ("_x", "_y")
    A lengthgth-2 sequence where each element is optiontotal_ally a string
    indicating the suffix to add to overlapping column names in
    `left` and `right` respectively. Pass a value of `None` instead
    of a string to indicate that the column name from `left` or
    `right` should be left as-is, with no suffix. At least one of the
    values must not be None.
clone : bool, default True

indicator : bool or str, default False
    If True, adds a column to the output KnowledgeFrame ctotal_alled "_unioner" with
    informatingion on the source of each row. The column can be given a different
    name by providing a string argument. The column will have a Categorical
    type with the value of "left_only" for observations whose unioner key only
    appears in the left KnowledgeFrame, "right_only" for observations

        Objects passed to the function are Collections objects whose index is
        either the KnowledgeFrame's index (``axis=0``) or the KnowledgeFrame's columns
        (``axis=1``). By default (``result_type=None``), the final return type
        is inferred from the return type of the applied function. Otherwise,
        it depends on the `result_type` argument.

        Parameters
        ----------
        func : function
            Function to employ to each column or row.
        axis : {0 or 'index', 1 or 'columns'}, default 0
            Axis along which the function is applied:

            * 0 or 'index': employ function to each column.
            * 1 or 'columns': employ function to each row.

        raw : bool, default False
            Detergetting_mines if row or column is passed as a Collections or ndarray object:

            * ``False`` : passes each row or column as a Collections to the
              function.
            * ``True`` : the passed function will receive ndarray objects
              instead.
              If you are just employing a NumPy reduction function this will
              achieve much better performance.

        result_type : {'expand', 'reduce', 'broadcast', None}, default None
            These only act when ``axis=1`` (columns):

            * 'expand' : list-like results will be turned into columns.
            * 'reduce' : returns a Collections if possible rather than expanding
              list-like results. This is the opposite of 'expand'.

              of the KnowledgeFrame, the original index and columns will be

            applied function: list-like results will be returned as a Collections
